A California Apple user has filed a class action lawsuit accusing Apple of making misleading claims about the privacy protection of its "Hide My Email" feature. Read on for details.

Apple Sued Over Alleged 'Hide My Email' Vulnerability

As 404 Media previously reported, Apple was made aware of a vulnerability more than a year ago that could potentially expose the real email address behind a "Hide My Email" alias.

Apple's "Hide My Email" feature lets users create unique, randomly generated email addresses that forward messages to their personal inbox, making it easy to sign up for apps, websites, and newsletters without revealing your real email address.

The feature is offered for free through "Sign in with Apple," and iCloud+ subscribers (starting at $0.99/month) get a fuller version that lets them create aliases for websites, newsletters, and other services.

According to 404 Media, a security researcher alerted Apple in June 2025 to a vulnerability that could potentially expose the real email addresses behind "Hide My Email" aliases.

Apple acknowledged receiving the report about a month later, but is said to have failed to fix the issue. In March 2026, the company said it had patched the vulnerability, but the researcher found it was still exploitable.

404 Media's report:

Regarding the lawsuit (reported by MacRumors), plaintiff Anthony Alvarez said:

Apple has been aware of this problem for over a year and yet the vulnerability remains unfixed—while Apple continues to profit from "Hide My Email" and its privacy promises. Plaintiff is one of millions of customers who paid for iCloud+ and trusted Apple's claim that "Hide My Email" would protect their personal email addresses. Plaintiff and the class paid for privacy—iCloud+ subscribers through the premium portion of their iCloud+ subscription fee, and all Apple customers through the product premiums Apple charges for features such as its purported enhanced privacy protections.

The lawsuit also claims this isn't an isolated incident, citing a 2023 report that Apple’s randomized MAC address feature could potentially expose users' real hardware identifying numbers.

The complaint also alleges the proposed class members are seeking more than $5 million in total damages (not including interest and costs), but doesn't explain how that number was calculated.

Alvarez is suing on behalf of himself and other Apple customers he claims have been similarly affected. He is asking the court to certify the case as a class action covering four proposed groups of users:

  • All Apple customers nationwide who purchased a device and used "Hide My Email";
  • A California subgroup of those users;
  • All iCloud+ subscribers nationwide who used the feature;
  • A California subgroup of iCloud+ subscribers.

He is seeking a jury trial and, in addition to monetary damages to be determined, wants the court to order Apple to fix the "Hide My Email" feature or clearly disclose its limitations.

Apple has not yet responded to the lawsuit.

Do you think this class action should be certified? Let us know in the comments.
